pll1d31c1-d1e3501.summary: Asks whether the coequality of the persons is said relatively or substantially, whether equality concerns relation or essence, and what equality is.

pll1d31c1-d1e3504.summary: Answers that as nothing is similar to itself (Hilary), nothing is equal to itself, so 'equal,' like 'similar,' is said relatively: the Son is equal to the Father and the Spirit to both.

pll1d31c1-d1e3521.summary: Adds that the Son is equal to the Father and the Spirit to both because of the supreme simplicity and unity of essence; so equality is by substance, not relation.
claims: The persons are equal by substance.

pll1d31c1-d1e3525.summary: Cites De Trinitate V: the Son is not equal according to what is said relative to the Father; so he is equal according to what is said 'ad se,' which is substance; so they have the same substance.
claims: The Son is equal to the Father according to substance.
Father and Son have the same substance.

pll1d31c1-d1e3543.summary: Cites De Trinitate VI: if the Son were unequal in anything that signifies his substance, he would not be equal at all; so he is equal in all and of the same substance, and so is the Spirit, because of supreme simplicity. So the persons are equal by substance and only the name is relative.
claims: The Son is equal to the Father in all things.
The Spirit is equal to both.
Only the name of equality is relative.

pll1d31c1-d1e3564.summary: Concludes that the equality of Father and Son is not a relation or notion but non-disparity due to unity of nature.
claims: Equality among the persons is not a relation or notion.
It is non-disparity from unity of nature.

pll1d31c1-d1e3569.summary: Says the same of 'similar' and likeness: 'the Son is similar to the Father' is relative, but he is similar by unity of essence, so the name is relative and the likeness is undifferentiated essence.
claims: Likeness among the persons is undifferentiated essence.

pll1d31c1-d1e3583.summary: Reports that some hold, not unlearnedly, that equality and likeness remove rather than posit: the Son is equal because neither greater nor less, similar because not diverse, alien, or dissimilar, by unity and simplicity of essence. So the Son is not equal or similar insofar as begotten, but by substance.
claims: The Son is equal and similar by substance, not by being begotten.

pl-l1d31c1.summary: Asks whether coequality is said relatively or substantially and what equality is. Like 'similar,' 'equal' is relative, since nothing is equal to itself (Hilary). Yet the Son is equal to the Father, and the Spirit to both, because of the supreme simplicity and unity of essence, so by substance, not relation (Augustine). Equality of Father and Son is not a relation or notion but non-disparity due to unity of nature; likewise likeness is undifferentiated essence. Some say, not unlearnedly, that equality and likeness remove rather than posit: the Son is equal because neither greater nor less, and similar because not diverse or alien.
claims: 'Equal' and 'similar' are relative terms, since nothing is equal or similar to itself.
The Son is equal to the Father, and the Spirit to both, by substance, not relation.
Equality among the persons is not a relation or notion but non-disparity from unity of nature.
Likeness among the persons is undifferentiated essence.
Equality and likeness may be understood as removing inequality and difference rather than positing something.
